answer: SES (Socioeconomic Status) is the unique target whose effect on BA-degree completion flips from approximately +0.36 (significant) in the SES-only baseline to approximately -0.23 (insignificant) when both race and academic characteristics are added jointly. Concrete evidence from the logit / HC1 model on N=8773 complete-case respondents (z-scored continuous predictors, race ref = White): M1 SES coef = +0.3511 log-odds per 1-SD (95% CI +0.238,+0.464; p = 1.04e-09; raw SES scale +0.4729 per unit). M2 SES = +0.2616 (p = 7.48e-05). M3 SES = -0.1720 (95% CI -0.334,-0.010; p = 0.0375; raw SES scale -0.2316 per unit, practically identical to the benchmark's -0.2293). M4 SES = +0.2191 (p = 0.0122). No other candidate (SAMPLE_SEX, FAMILY SIZE OF SAMPLE, ABILITY, PERCENTILE IN CLASS) shows a sign-flip-plus-significance-loss. The flip is estimator-invariant (logit -0.1720, probit -0.0697 with p = 0.065, standardized-LPM -0.0047 with p = 0.039), race-reference invariant (switching White to Black leaves the SES coefficient identical), HC1 vs HC3 identical, robust to academic-block specification (PERCENTILE-only gives -0.0025 with p = 0.97 under both race refs), and not driven by multicollinearity (SES VIF = 1.37, max VIF = 2.58).
